source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs about a hidden user preference far worse than a Bayesian assistant. Most stop improving after round 1.
numbers: Flight-recommendation task, 5 rounds, 624 simulated users. Final-round accuracy for the off-the-shelf LLMs is roughly 36 to 58 percent, against 81 percent for the Bayesian assistant. Humans (48 users) rose from round 1 to 5 (p=0.002) but also fell short.
quote: LLMs fall far short of the standard defined by the Bayesian framework.
limits: Preference inference over a small discrete hypothesis set, not open-ended evidence. Accuracy values read from a bar chart.
agent_relevance: Plain LLMs do not accumulate evidence across turns. The scaffold should hold the running belief in code and not trust the model to carry it.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Prompt-level fixes did not help. Chain-of-thought, numeric option formats, 30 rounds instead of 5, and base (non-instruct) models all failed to give meaningful gains.
numbers: Appendix C.1 list: CoT prompting, purely numerical option encoding, 30 rounds, pre-trained-only models. No meaningful improvement reported for any.
limits: Flight task only. Open-weight Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5 plus GPT-4.1 Mini and Gemini 1.5 Pro.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to reason step by step does not fix evidence weighting. Supports doing probability updates in code (guardrail G5).

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Fine-tuning on the Bayesian assistant's guesses beats fine-tuning on the correct answers (oracle) and generalises to hotel and web-shopping tasks.
numbers: Bayesian-tuned LLMs agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80 percent of the time, more than original or oracle-tuned models. Bayesian teaching gave higher accuracy and less variance than oracle teaching. Gap narrower on web shopping.
limits: Needs training, so outside our no-training scaffold. Teacher is a hand-built Bayesian model on a small hypothesis space.
agent_relevance: Shows the skill can be taught, but our agent has no training. Compare AdaptFuse (c24), which gets a similar effect without training.

source: Filbry, Melo, Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
finding: Direct belief updating in context violates Bayes rule. Probabilities elicited in separate conversations are often incoherent, but within one dialogue they are mostly coherent.
numbers: Dutch-book test, 30 scenarios: across separate conversations violation rates exceeded 50 percent of scenarios for almost all model and axiom pairs. Within one dialogue they fell to 10 percent for Gemini and 1 scenario of 30 for Gemma. Without reasoning, LLM updates cut final success by at least 30 percent versus the Bayesian oracle in 20 Questions (40 animals) and ProteinWorld (40 runs); weak models near 0 percent on 20Q.
limits: Small open models (Qwen-2.5-32B, Phi-4, Gemma-4 variants) plus Gemini-2.5-Pro. Toy worlds where likelihoods are fully specified.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to S7. Keep earlier judgments visible in the same dialogue, and keep the running probabilities in code.

source: Filbry, Melo, Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors
finding: Reasoning mode pushes posterior error (KL) close to zero on the simple task, and a Python tool does the same on a hard, intractable posterior.
numbers: Reasoning on: KL falls strongly on 20Q and nears 0 on ProteinWorld-simple for the three models with a reasoning mode. Gemini-2.5-Pro with Python on ProteinWorld-hard: KL and the posterior-mass gap to the oracle close to 0, matching the oracle.
limits: Only 3 models had a reasoning mode; one model for the tool test. 5 worlds, 8 hypotheses, 6 experiments.
agent_relevance: Cheap evidence that reasoning plus a calculator tool beats a bare prompt for weighing evidence across hypotheses.

source: Samanta et al. (2026) BayesBench: LLM Belief Trajectories Under Multi-Turn Evidence Accumulation
finding: A bookbag-and-poker-chip style test for LLMs (after Phillips and Edwards 1966). Small models under-update, larger models over-update toward extremes when evidence is skewed.
numbers: Seven models: Llama 3 at 3B, 8B, 70B and Qwen 2.5 at 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B. Tasks: coin bias estimation, movie rating from user type, Reddit social judgment, medical triage. Better latent inference did not carry over to calibrated predictions.
quote: Models are capable of Bayesian-aligned evidence accumulation
limits: Mean absolute error tables not copied. Single-turn versus multi-turn delivery changes small-model results.
agent_relevance: Reproduces the human conservatism pattern in small models and the reverse in large ones. Do not trust the size of the model's own update. Use computed likelihood ratios.

source: Samanta et al. (2026) BayesBench
finding: Active conversation with a user makes models more pro-user than passive reading of the same evidence.
numbers: Social judgment: behaviour rated as unwarranted by the evidence 72 percent under defending framing, 60 percent neutral, 56 percent conceding. Models echo the poster's framing on 41 to 99 percent of turns.
limits: Judged by a third-party LLM judge. Reddit verdict task only.
agent_relevance: Evidence is weighted differently depending on who offers it. For S7 keep the evidence-reading step blind to who proposed the hypothesis (G5).

source: Batista and Griffiths (2026) A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI
finding: In a modified Wason 2-4-6 task, a default GPT chatbot mostly gave hypothesis-confirming examples, and discovery was about a fifth of the rate under unbiased sampling.
numbers: N=557, 504 gave a final hypothesis. Discovery rates: random-sequence feedback 29.5 percent, rule-disconfirming 14.1, agreeable 11.8, rule-confirming 8.4, default GPT 5.9 (diff to random 23.6 points). Confidence rose +5.4 in default GPT (p=.009) while random-sequence fell 56.8. Preregistered.
quote: Unmodified LLM behavior suppressed discovery and inflated confidence comparably to explicitly sycophantic prompting.
limits: Humans talking to an LLM, three rounds. Default GPT versus rule-confirming difference not significant (2.5 points, 95 percent CI -4.6 to 9.6).
agent_relevance: A confirming data source adds confidence but no information. Test results must come from a source that does not know the favoured hypothesis (G3, G4).

source: Batista and Griffiths (2026) A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI
finding: Bayesian model: if data are sampled conditional on the user's hypothesis, beliefs do not move toward the truth but confidence in the (possibly wrong) hypothesis grows. No bias in the person is needed.
numbers: Proof sketch in paper. Also cites sycophancy rates: 58.2 percent of medical and maths queries (Fanous 2025); 63.7 percent mean agreement with a stated wrong opinion across seven model families, range 46.6 to 95.1 (Wang 2025).
limits: The cited rates are secondary, taken from this paper's introduction, not checked at source.
agent_relevance: Formal reason that a test chosen by the hypothesis itself has no diagnostic value, which is the core of S7.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: Twelve LLMs play a Wason-style semantic rule game. Models that test outside their hypothesis (negative tests) succeed much more often.
numbers: Best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41 percent success; reasoning models GPT-5.2-Chat 75 percent and GPT-OSS-120B 68 percent; other instruct models 33 to 35 percent; GPT-5-Nano 12 and Qwen3.5-9B 21. Confirmation bias (share of positive tests): reasoning models about 24 to 39 percent, instruct models 66 to 82 percent. Bayesian mixed model on n=1,200 games: confirmation-bias coefficient -4.15 (OR 0.016); oracle error had no credible effect.
quote: models that actively seek to falsify their hypotheses consistently outperform those that primarily seek confirmation
limits: Semantic taxonomy games built so the hypothesis is narrower than the rule. Models were both player and oracle. Small reasoning models did worse than instruct models.
agent_relevance: Strong measured case that an explicit negative-test step is the main lever. Build S7 to force a test the leading hypothesis predicts will fail.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench
finding: Turn-level view: the share of tests that could conclusively falsify the current hypothesis follows the same order as success.
numbers: Conclusive falsification rate per test turn: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2 percent, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5; lowest Llama-4-Maverick 18.0 and GPT-5-Nano 26.6. Oracle agreement with human annotators about 85 to 95 percent.
limits: Hypothesis-to-rule relation was labelled by an LLM annotator, not by humans.
agent_relevance: A measurable per-turn metric the agent could log: share of tests that could have falsified the current hypothesis.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT: Wason Inductive Logic Test
finding: Multi-turn hidden-function task. All tested LLMs struggle. The best solves 28 percent. Failures are repeated tests, uninformative tests and unlikely guesses.
numbers: 50 rules, up to 30 test cases each. Solved: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50, o1-mini 13/50, o1-preview 12/50, chatgpt-4o-latest 11/50, Mistral Large 2 11/50, GPT-4o 9/50, Llama 3.1 405B 8/50, Gemini 1.5 Pro 5/50, Claude 3 Haiku 1/50, Gemini 1.5 Flash 8b 0/50.
limits: Boolean rules over three integers. 2024 models; newer models not tested.
agent_relevance: Older baseline on the same Wason paradigm as c10. Weakness is both choosing tests and drawing the conclusion.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT
finding: Swapping test cases between models shows test selection and inference are separate skills. o1-mini guessed 19 of 50 rules given chatgpt-4o-latest's test cases.
numbers: o1-mini alone 13/50; with chatgpt-4o-latest tests 19/50. Models differ in how useful their tests are to other models.
limits: Post-hoc cross-model pairing on one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting S7 into a test-proposer slot and a separate evidence-reader slot, with code between them.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Choosing the question by expected information gain over the model's own sampled candidate answers beats asking the model to write a good question.
numbers: 20 Questions, GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o-mini: EIG with uniform weights ranked above EIG with log-probs, implicit and implicit-ToT strategies (15 animals, 5 seeds, 25 evaluation seeds). Code tasks (48 non-trivial tasks): EIG strategies reached higher accuracy with fewer test cases. Zero-shot GPT-4o-mini scored 35 percent on APPS.
limits: Gap shrinks for stronger models. Uses about 20 sampled solutions and more LLM calls. Author list from the page header only partly read.
agent_relevance: A cheap sample-then-score design for S7: sample candidate hypotheses, ask which question splits them best, count in code.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT simulates answers, scores each question by information gain, and picks the best path. It lifts success in diagnosis, troubleshooting and 20 Questions.
numbers: Average +38.1 percent success over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs; +46.6 percent for Llama3-70B. DX medical 97.0 percent with GPT-4; MedDG 81.4 (Gemini-1.5-Pro) and 88.0 (GPT-4). Troubleshooting 43.7 to 67.3 percent. UoT beat CoT-SC by 33.8 and Reflexion by 29.9.
limits: Small closed answer sets. Simulated patients. Gains are relative percentages.
agent_relevance: Closest direct use of diagnosticity (information gain) inside an LLM loop. Strong support for S7 as expected-information-gain question choice.

source: Bickford Smith, Kirchhof, Zhang, Rainforth (2026) BED-LLM (ICLR 2026)
finding: Choosing queries by expected information gain computed from the LLM's own predictive distribution roughly doubles success on 20 Questions versus plain prompting.
numbers: Mean +37.4 percentage points over direct prompting; success more than doubled in over half the setups and never fell. Animals set, 100 targets: GPT-4o-mini 44 to 88 percent; GPT-4o 45 to 93; Llama-3.1-8B 8 to 63; Qwen2.5-72B 45 to 95.
limits: The way EIG is built (conditioning on full history) mattered. Needs many LLM calls. Movie preference task showed smaller gains.
agent_relevance: A tested recipe: keep an explicit set of hypotheses, update it after each answer, pick the question with highest EIG. Matches S7 plus a belief state.

source: Bickford Smith et al. (2026) BED-LLM
finding: Even a crude splitting rule beats model-written questions, but full EIG is better. CoT-prompted questions help only a little.
numbers: Animals, GPT-4o-mini: Prompt-only 44, Split 78, CoT 55, BED-LLM 88 percent. Llama-3.1-8B: 8, 49, 19, 63.
limits: Table values read from the text extract; other datasets show smaller gaps.
agent_relevance: Split-in-half is a cheap fallback if full EIG is too costly.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: Letting the LM ask open questions or write edge cases to label elicits preferences better than users writing prompts or labelling examples.
numbers: Three domains. GATE beat user-written prompts in 6 of 10 settings (absolute) and 7 of 10 (area under curve). Generative yes/no questions beat user prompts in every setting studied. Significance only in content recommendation and email verification.
limits: Moderate power. Prompted, not information-gain based. Moral reasoning domain underpowered.
agent_relevance: Edge-case generation is a form of asking for the most diagnostic example. Suggests a step that asks for cases where candidate readings disagree.

source: Liao, Deng, Ren (2026) Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis
finding: Audit of how five open LLMs weigh evidence pieces. Most interactions are faithful support or conflict between competing diagnoses, but absent or negated findings are where shortcut-like errors cluster.
numbers: DDXPlus, CupCase, MedCase. Conflict or cancellation make up 86.6 to 89.6 percent of DDXPlus interaction strength in the main setting; negated or absent misuse 1.2 to 3.0 percent. Blinded review of 130 items by five reviewers: invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated findings; all five agreed on 77 percent.
limits: Behavioural audit; automatic labels are screening signals only. Open-weight models only. Percentages summarised from the text extract.
agent_relevance: Absence of a finding is diagnostic only relative to a specific hypothesis, and models mishandle it. S7 should record what a missing result would mean for each hypothesis.

source: Wei and Fink (2026) AgentRCA: Agentic Root Cause Analysis through Evidence-Grounded Reasoning
finding: Requiring a ranked hypothesis table raised diagnostic accuracy over free tool use and over a ReAct-style loop.
numbers: PRONTO facility, five operating states. Top-1: no reasoning structure 83.2 percent (Top-2 93.3), ReAct-like 85.4 (95.6), hypothesis table 87.6 (96.8). Supervised LightGBM 99.0, autoencoder 99.6, MiniRocket 94.5. With few labels the best supervised model fell to 65.1 percent.
limits: Industrial sensor data with a digital twin. Same model across arms. Zero-shot means no fault examples.
agent_relevance: Direct scaffold ablation of the ACH-style hypothesis table. About 4 points from structure alone.

source: Wei and Fink (2026) AgentRCA
finding: System-prompt guidance on how to read each evidence tool added accuracy, and short domain rules aimed at common misdiagnoses added more.
numbers: Three prompt arms on PRONTO: no guidance, zero-shot guidance (default, 87.6 percent), error-guided rules. Accuracy rose with task-specific guidance.
limits: Exact values for the non-default arms were not legible in the text extract.
agent_relevance: Telling the model what each kind of evidence can and cannot discriminate improves results. A per-domain evidence-meaning note is cheap.

source: Marozzo, Lio et al. (2026) LLM-as-an-Investigator: Evidence-First Agentic Reasoning for Robust Interactive Problem Diagnosis
finding: A multi-role agent that keeps competing hypotheses, challenges the leader with counterfactual questions and verifies at the end scores higher than direct, thinking, ReAct and Tree-of-Thought baselines.
numbers: 100 cases from 303 forum threads. Final score out of 100: SIA 79.2 [72.7, 83.7], THK-int 72.8, Ask-5 72.3, ReAct 69.0, ToT 61.5, BAS 67.3. Other backbones: GPT-5.6 Terra 75.4 vs 69.2; Claude Sonnet 5 76.1 vs 68.4.
limits: Final score still 10 points below candidate-pool potential (89.2): the right cause was often present but not selected. Descriptive differences, small cohort. Author order not checked.
agent_relevance: Selection, not generation, is the weak spot. Supports a separate adjudication step that reads recorded evidence.

source: Marozzo, Lio et al. (2026) LLM-as-an-Investigator
finding: Ablation: dropping structured investigation or counterfactual critique costs the most. Evidence-based weight updates matter least.
numbers: Full 79.2. Without structured investigation 72.8; without counterfactual critique 74.0; without follow-up questions 75.0; without final adjudication 76.0; without hypothesis expansion 76.5 (potential 89.2 to 79.3); without weight updates 78.5. Misleading user suggestion, 10 paired cases: wrong cause chosen 2 of 10; score 80.0 to 76.0.
limits: One backbone for the ablation, small paired sample (10).
agent_relevance: Counterfactual challenge of the leading hypothesis was worth more than numeric weighting here. Supports S7 as challenge-first.

source: Lin et al. (2026) AdaptFuse: Training-Free Sequential Preference Inference via Externalized Bayesian Computation
finding: A symbolic module holds the Bayesian posterior and a frozen LLM only supplies preference signals. This matches or slightly beats Bayesian-teaching fine-tuning with no training.
numbers: Flight accuracy on Gemma after 5 rounds: self-consistency 44.7, Oracle Learning 59.1, Bayesian Teaching 73.4, AdaptFuse 76.2; no-EMA ablation 74.0 (0.6 over Bayesian Teaching). Gains over Bayesian Teaching 2.8 (Gemma), 2.0 (Llama), 2.1 (Qwen). Cost 4.35 to 4.63 s per round versus 1.05 to 1.42 s.
limits: Needs a hand-specified likelihood and a hypothesis set (authors say so). Much of the margin disappears without the EMA step. Ablation only on Gemma.
agent_relevance: Best match to our design: code keeps the posterior, the model supplies evidence readings. The G5 principle, now measured.

source: Agarwal et al. (2026) Evidence-Informed LLM Beliefs for Continual Scientific Discovery
finding: Surprise measured as belief shift after seeing evidence (used as a discovery reward) is partly an artifact when the prior never changes. Retrieval over past discoveries fixes much of it.
numbers: 37.5 percent of static surprisals were spurious. Belief-update filtering and diversity raised accumulated non-stationary surprisal by 30.62 percent on average over five domains.
limits: Abstract and method read; full tables not checked. Specific to AutoDiscovery-style loops.
agent_relevance: If the agent uses prior-to-posterior shift as a sign that a test was informative, refresh the priors from earlier results first, or the shift is inflated.

source: Position paper (2024) Diagnostic uncertainty estimation from LLMs: next-word probability is not pre-test probability
finding: Probabilities read from token logits or verbalised confidence are poor estimates of clinical pre-test probability.
numbers: Token-logit mean AUROC 49.9 (95 percent CI 47.8 to 51.9); verbalised confidence 50.9 (48.7 to 53.1). Embeddings plus a small trained model did much better, nearly matching raw-data XGBoost for sepsis. Positive-class rates 43, 16, 11 percent for three diagnoses; Mistral-7B and Llama3-70B.
limits: Medical tabular tasks, two open models. Author list not read.
agent_relevance: Do not take the model's stated confidence as p(E|H). Use computed or externally checked likelihoods.

source: Lei and Cooper (2026) Elicitation Matters: How Prompts and Query Protocols Shape LLM Surrogates under Sparse Observations
finding: How belief is asked for changes the belief. Pointwise and joint queries give different uncertainty, and sequential evidence gives order-sensitive, non-monotonic confidence.
numbers: Qualitative in the abstract; changes downstream acquisition decisions and regret in Bayesian optimisation tests (numbers not extracted).
limits: Regression surrogate setting, not hypothesis tests. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Order and format of evidence can move confidence. For S7, fix the presentation order and re-ask in a second order as a check.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM: Collaborative Decision-Making via ACH-Inspired Structured Reasoning
finding: Prompts a decision agent to build a hypotheses-by-evidence matrix (consistent, inconsistent, irrelevant), re-check the ratings, and pick the hypothesis with the fewest inconsistencies; then trains the model to do it.
numbers: MMLU-Pro: AgentCDM 65.2 versus Qwen-7B-R1 58.0. Heterogeneous agent pool: MMLU-Pro 67.9 vs 55.9 for Qwen-7B-Instruct with the ACH prompt; MMLU 78.9 vs 75.2; ARC-Challenge 93.0 vs 87.2.
limits: Multi-agent answer selection on multiple-choice tests, not intelligence-style evidence. Training needed. Stage ablation not matched to arms and so not reported.
agent_relevance: The only LLM paper found that names ACH directly. The plain ACH prompt (matrix then fewest inconsistencies) exists as a reusable baseline.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 8 (ACH)
finding: ACH ranks hypotheses by how little evidence contradicts them, and says evidence consistent with all hypotheses has no diagnostic value.
numbers: Not opened this session. Recalled only.
limits: From memory, not verified here. No LLM test of the matrix method as a standalone scaffold was found in this search.
agent_relevance: Reference point for what the S7 step should emulate; check against the angle A and B documents.
